source_refs.note: Book p. 5: 1.3.2 Non-Fundamental Transcendental Functions, examples, Examples 5 and 6

blocks.text: Functions formed by combining transcendental functions with algebraic functions, or by applying transformations and composition, are non-fundamental transcendental functions.

\(y = \sin x + \ln x\), \(y = e^{x^{2}}\), \(y = x \sin x\), \(y = \ln 2x\) are examples of functions which are not fundamental transcendental functions. On the other hand, \(y = 10^{2x}\) is a standard transcental function, because, it can be written as \(y = 100^{x}\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "standard transcental function"; the correct word is "transcendental": \(y = 10^{2x}\) is a standard (fundamental) transcendental function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(10^{2x}\) fundamental but \(e^{x^{2}}\) not? Use the law \((a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}\):
\[10^{2x} = (10^{2})^{x} = 100^{x}\]
This is exactly the form \(a^{x}\) with \(a = 100\). But \(e^{x^{2}}\) cannot be written as \(a^{x}\) for any constant \(a\), because its exponent is \(x^{2}\), not a constant multiple of \(x\): it is the composition of \(e^{u}\) with \(u = x^{2}\).
How each example is built: \(\sin x + \ln x\) (sum of two standard functions), \(x \sin x\) (product with the algebraic function \(x\)), \(e^{x^{2}}\) (composition), \(\ln 2x\) (composition with \(2x\); a transformation of \(\ln x\), since \(\ln 2x = \ln 2 + \ln x\) for \(x > 0\)).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Before deciding "non-fundamental", always try to rewrite the function as one standard function. For example \(4^{x/2} = (4^{1/2})^{x} = 2^{x}\) is fundamental. If no rewriting works, name the extra operation (sum, product, composition or added constant) in your answer.

blocks.title: Example 5
blocks.problem:
Given the following functions:
\(f(x) = \sqrt{x+1}\), \(g(x) = e^{x}\), \(h(x) = \frac{x+1}{x^{2}-2x+1}\), \(q(x) = \ln 2x\), \(r(x) = \sin x\).
Classify each function as algebraic or transcendental.
steps:
Given: five functions \(f, g, h, q, r\).
To find: which are algebraic and which are transcendental.
Method: a function is algebraic if it is made from \(x\) by finitely many \(+, -, \times, \div\) and roots (it then satisfies a polynomial equation in \(y\)); if \(x\) sits inside an exponential, logarithmic or trigonometric function, it is transcendental. We test each function in turn.

Step 1: \(f(x) = \sqrt{x+1}\)
\[y = \sqrt{x+1}\]
\[y^{2} - (x + 1) = 0\]
Why: only an addition and a square root are used, and squaring gives a polynomial equation in \(y\). So \(f\) is algebraic.

Step 2: \(h(x) = \frac{x+1}{x^{2}-2x+1}\)
\[(x^{2} - 2x + 1)\,y - (x + 1) = 0\]
Why: \(h\) is a quotient of two polynomials (a rational function), so multiplying by the denominator gives a polynomial equation in \(y\). So \(h\) is algebraic. (Since \(x^{2} - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^{2}\), \(h\) is defined for \(x \ne 1\).)

Step 3: \(g(x) = e^{x}\)
Why: the variable \(x\) is in the exponent; \(e^{x}\) is the natural exponential function. So \(g\) is transcendental.

Step 4: \(q(x) = \ln 2x\)
Why: \(x\) is inside a logarithm. So \(q\) is transcendental.

Step 5: \(r(x) = \sin x\)
Why: \(x\) is inside a trigonometric function. So \(r\) is transcendental.

Check: substitute back into the equations of Steps 1 and 2:
\[(\sqrt{x+1})^{2} - (x+1) = 0\]
\[(x^{2}-2x+1)\cdot\dfrac{x+1}{x^{2}-2x+1} - (x+1) = 0\]
Both hold, confirming that \(f\) and \(h\) are algebraic. Five functions: 2 algebraic + 3 transcendental.
blocks.answer: Algebraic functions: \(f(x) = \sqrt{x+1}\), \(h(x) = \frac{x+1}{x^{2}-2x+1}\). Transcendental functions: \(g(x) = e^{x}\), \(q(x) = \ln 2x\), \(r(x) = \sin x\).

blocks.title: Example 6
blocks.problem:
Given the following functions:
\(f(x) = \cos 2x + 1\), \(g(x) = 3^{x}\), \(h(x) = \tan^{-1} x^{2}\), \(q(x) = \ln x + e^{x}\), \(r(x) = \tan x\).
Classify each function as fundamental or non-fundamental transcendental functions.
steps:
Given: five transcendental functions \(f, g, h, q, r\).
To find: which are fundamental and which are non-fundamental.
Method: a function is fundamental if it is exactly one standard function (\(a^{x}\), \(\ln x\), a trigonometric or an inverse trigonometric function of \(x\) itself) or can be rewritten as one. If it combines functions, puts an expression other than \(x\) inside, or adds a constant, it is non-fundamental.

Step 1: \(g(x) = 3^{x}\)
\[g(x) = a^{x},\quad a = 3\]
Why: it is the standard exponential form with \(a = 3 > 0\), \(a \ne 1\). So \(g\) is fundamental.

Step 2: \(r(x) = \tan x\)
Why: \(\tan x\) is a standard trigonometric function of \(x\) itself, with nothing added or composed. So \(r\) is fundamental.

Step 3: \(f(x) = \cos 2x + 1\)
Why: the standard function \(\cos\) is applied to \(2x\) (a composition with the algebraic function \(2x\)) and then 1 is added (combination with an algebraic function). So \(f\) is non-fundamental.

Step 4: \(h(x) = \tan^{-1}(x^{2})\)
Why: the standard function \(\tan^{-1}\) is applied to \(x^{2}\), not to \(x\): a composition. So \(h\) is non-fundamental.

Step 5: \(q(x) = \ln x + e^{x}\)
Why: it is the sum of two different standard transcendental functions, so it is a combination. So \(q\) is non-fundamental.

Check: each fundamental answer matches one row of the standard families (exponential \(a^{x}\); trigonometric \(\tan x\)); each non-fundamental one needs an extra operation (\(+1\), \(2x\) inside, \(x^{2}\) inside, a sum) that no single standard function has. Five functions: 2 fundamental + 3 non-fundamental.
blocks.answer: Fundamental transcendental functions: \(g(x) = 3^{x}\), \(r(x) = \tan x\). Non-fundamental transcendental functions: \(f(x) = \cos 2x + 1\), \(h(x) = \tan^{-1}(x^{2})\), \(q(x) = \ln x + e^{x}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Non-fundamental transcendental functions are made from standard ones by combining with algebraic functions (sum, product), by transformations, or by composition.
2. A function that can be rewritten as a single standard form is fundamental: \(10^{2x} = 100^{x}\).
3. Examples 5 and 6 use two different questions: algebraic vs transcendental (Example 5), then fundamental vs non-fundamental (Example 6).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Calling \(10^{2x}\) non-fundamental only because of the \(2x\): rewrite it first, \(10^{2x} = 100^{x}\).
2. Calling \(e^{x^{2}}\) fundamental: \(e^{x^{2}} \ne (e^{x})^{2} = e^{2x}\); its exponent is \(x^{2}\), so it is a composition.
3. Forgetting the bracket in \(\tan^{-1} x^{2}\): it means \(\tan^{-1}(x^{2})\), not \((\tan^{-1} x)^{2}\).
